objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain when a missed approach is required, brief the missed approach from the chart, teach the initiation (power, climb attitude, drag) and the climb by instruments, plan and check missed approach climb gradients, teach the ATC report and what to say when unable to comply, fly early and circling missed approaches correctly, use the MFD and GPS on the missed, and demonstrate, explain, analyze and correct a learner's missed approach errors.
why: The missed approach comes when flight deck workload is at its maximum, so the procedure should be studied and mastered before the approach begins [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]. Its obstacle protection assumes it starts at the DA/DH or at the MAP not lower than the MDA, with a climb of at least 200 ft per NM and no abnormally early turn [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. A go-around is not inherently dangerous; it becomes dangerous only when delayed unduly or executed improperly [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Positive aircraft control and checklist usage are special emphasis areas on the checkride (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).

warmup: Think first: on a VOR approach your learner reaches the MDA 2 miles before the MAP, sees nothing, says "going missed" and starts the climbing right turn the chart shows. Climbing out, the airspeed decays, all the flaps come up at once, and nobody tells ATC. Which of these could hit an obstacle, which is a technique error, and what would you teach first?

key_terms.def: Begins at the MAP and ends at a point or fix where an initial or en route segment begins [[29:190|IPH 4-50]].
The DA/DH on a vertically guided approach; non-vertically guided and circling procedures share one MAP, found by timing from the FAF, a fix, a NAVAID or a waypoint [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f5]].
The GPS MAP, always a fly-over waypoint [[33:99|AIM 1-1-17b5(h)(3)]]; a non-WAAS receiver must be sequenced past it by the pilot [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(f)(1)]].
At least 200 ft per NM unless the chart notes publish a higher one, which ends at a stated altitude or fix [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]].
Gradient is feet per NM; the climb rate in feet per minute rises with groundspeed, and TPP tables convert one to the other [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]] [[29:34|IPH Figure 1-17]].
A missed approach started before the MAP; unless ATC clears otherwise, fly the procedure to the MAP at or above the MDA or DH before turning [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]].
A missed approach other than the published one, issued by ATC or put in effect by NOTAM, which makes it a mandatory part of the procedure [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21e]].
A go-around beyond the MAP or below the MDA or DA(H); the published missed then does not necessarily give obstacle clearance or separation [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]] [[33:453|AIM 5-4-21h]].

Quick-reference boxes in the profile that supplement the text; when space is short only the first four are shown, so they may not show the whole procedure [[2:115|Chart Users' Guide p 115]] [[33:419|AIM 5-4-5m7(c)]].
Finishing the missed approach climb in the holding pattern when the text says so, as in "continue climb-in-hold to 8000" [[29:187|IPH Figure 4-26]].
The belief that the approach is sure to end in a safe landing; with pride, a main source of delayed go-arounds [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
A rapid acceleration can feel like a nose-up attitude, and the disoriented pilot may push into a nose-low or dive attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

chunks.title: What the chart tells you about the missed approach

body.p: The Instrument lesson IR.VI.C covers flying the missed approach as a pilot, and lesson FII.VIII.A covers the nonprecision approach that leads to it. This lesson adds how you teach the missed approach, set it up safely and fix a learner's errors.

**Pertinent information on the selected instrument approach chart.** The missed approach is shown in three places: the full text in the middle briefing strip, the hatched track with an arrow in the plan view, and quick-reference icons in the profile [[2:115|Chart Users' Guide p 115]].

The text names the NAVAIDs or radials that define the fix [[23:42|IFH 1-23]]

body.p: The text uses a few standard forms: climb straight ahead ("Climb to 2,000"), a climbing turn ("Climbing right turn to 2,000"), or a straight climb to an initial altitude and then a turn toward the holding fix [[23:40|IFH 1-21]] [[23:42|IFH 1-23]]. The holding fix is often an IAF, so another approach can start without flying from the hold to an IAF, and ATC normally gives further instructions before the airplane gets there [[29:181|IPH 4-41]].

Two quieter items also belong in the briefing. A snowflake icon marks a Cold Temperature Airport [[33:419|AIM 5-4-5m7(f)(2)]]; when cold temperature correction applies to missed approach segments, the pilot tells ATC the intent and the amount on initial contact or as soon as possible [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a5]]. And on a GPS approach the MAWP is always a fly-over waypoint [[33:99|AIM 1-1-17b5(h)(3)]].

callout.text: Application: have the learner read the missed approach text aloud, then point to each step in the icons and in the plan view. Brief it even when the tower will probably give other instructions [[29:182|IPH 4-42]].

check.q: Your learner briefs the missed approach only from the profile icons. Why is that not enough?
check.a: When space is short only the first four icons are shown, so they may not show the whole procedure; the complete text is in the middle briefing strip [[2:115|Chart Users' Guide p 115]] [[33:419|AIM 5-4-5m7(c)]].

chunks.title: A chart to brief: Daggett RNAV (GPS) RWY 26

body.p: Practice on a demanding chart. The Daggett chart puts almost every missed approach item on one page [[29:187|IPH Figure 4-26]].

head: Item
On the Daggett chart
rows: Missed approach text
Climb to 8000 direct AMAKE and on track 270° to BINTE and on track 192° to NULMN and hold, continue climb-in-hold to 8000 [[29:187|IPH Figure 4-26]]

#Missed approach requires minimum climb of 220 feet per NM to 8000 [[29:187|IPH Figure 4-26]]

LPV DA # 2217-1 (HAT 299) needs the 220 ft/NM climb; LPV DA 2438-1¾ (HAT 520) does not [[29:187|IPH Figure 4-26]] [[29:181|IPH 4-41]]

Airport elevation 1930, TDZE 1918, MSA 7600 within 25 NM [[29:187|IPH Figure 4-26]]

Los Angeles Center 132.5; UNICOM 123.0 is the CTAF [[29:187|IPH Figure 4-26]]

body.p: **Teach what the two LPV lines mean.** When a missed needs more than 200 ft/NM, some charts publish two sets of minimums: the lower set requires the steeper climb, the higher set does not [[29:181|IPH 4-41]]. So the learner must check climb performance before choosing the 2217 line [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. Other charts solve it another way: at Burbank, an airplane that cannot make the ILS RWY 8 gradient uses the separately published LOC Y RWY 8, with higher minimums that meet the standard 200 ft/NM [[29:181|IPH 4-41]] [[29:186|IPH Figure 4-25]].

**Failure to have essential knowledge of the information on the instrument approach chart.** In the airplane it looks like a learner who climbs straight ahead with no idea of the next fix, turns the wrong way at the MAP, levels at the wrong altitude, or flies the LPV DA # line without checking the gradient. The usual cause is a briefing that stopped at the minimums. The fix is to study and master the missed before the approach starts, because it comes when workload is at its maximum [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]; most pilots brief the specific missed approach procedure aloud so it is fresh in mind [[29:182|IPH 4-42]]. Application: before the FAF, ask the learner for the first two steps of the missed from memory.

callout.text: The Daggett and other handbook charts here date from 2010 to 2011 and are marked not for navigation [[29:187|IPH Figure 4-26]]. Use them to teach chart reading; brief and fly only current charts.

check.q: Your learner plans the Daggett LPV DA # line at 2217 but has not looked at the airplane's climb data. What do you teach?
check.a: That line needs a climb of at least 220 ft per NM to 8000 [[29:187|IPH Figure 4-26]], and pilots must preplan that the airplane can meet it [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. If it cannot, use the higher LPV DA line, which needs no steeper gradient [[29:181|IPH 4-41]].

chunks.title: When a missed approach is required

body.p: **Conditions requiring a missed approach.** 14 CFR 91.175(e) makes it a rule, not a choice. The 91.175(c) conditions for going below the DA/DH or MDA are three: continuously in position to descend to the intended runway at a normal rate with normal maneuvers, flight visibility not less than the published value, and at least one listed visual reference distinctly visible and identifiable [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(c)]] [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.175(e): immediately execute an appropriate missed approach (1) when the 91.175(c) requirements are not met while below the MDA, or on arrival at the MAP (including a DA/DH) and at any time after that until touchdown; or (2) when an identifiable part of the airport is not distinctly visible during a circling maneuver at or above the MDA, unless only a normal bank hides it [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]] [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]].

body.p: **Failure to recognize conditions requiring a missed approach.** What you see: the learner levels off at the DA, or sits at the MDA past the MAP looking for the runway, or keeps descending on a few lights without the visibility. The usual causes are landing expectancy, the belief that the approach is sure to end with a safe landing, and pride, the belief that going around admits failure [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. The fix is a decision made before the FAF and said aloud: "At the MAP without a listed reference and the visibility, missed approach." Teach early that any approach may end in a go-around, and that blaming it on poor skill is a fallacy [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

callout.text: Application: make the learner say the trigger, not just the altitude: "Minimums, no lights, missed approach." A decision rehearsed on every approach is ready when it is real.

check.q: At the MAP on a LOC approach your learner sees the REIL flashing but judges flight visibility at half the chart value. The tower reports visibility at minimums. What is the call?
check.a: Missed approach. Flight visibility must not be less than the published value, and only the pilot judges it, whatever the report says [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(2)]] [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].

chunks.title: Starting the missed: power, climb attitude, less drag

body.p: **Initiation of the missed approach, including the prompt application of power, establishment of a climb attitude, and reduction of drag.** The IFH sequence: establish a climb pitch attitude while setting climb power, configure for climb, turn to the right heading, advise ATC and request further clearance [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]. The AFH gives the same three cardinal principles in order: power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

head: Step
What to teach
Why
rows: Power
Full or maximum allowable power, smoothly and without hesitation; carburetor heat off, as applicable [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
A settling airplane has inertia, and power stops the descent; abrupt throttle movement can make some engines falter [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Climb attitude
Hold forward elevator pressure and right rudder as the power comes in, then rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Added power raises the nose and yaws left; a nose that rises too early can cause an unrecoverable stall when low [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Drag: flaps
Once the descent has stopped, retract the flaps partly or to the takeoff setting the manufacturer recommends, in small steps [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
A sudden, complete retraction can cause a loss of lift and settling [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Drag: gear
Up after a positive rate of climb, once rough trim is done and the airplane will stay airborne; flaps at least partly up first unless the AFM/POH says otherwise [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]
Full flaps usually make more drag than the gear, and gear down protects an accidental touchdown [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]

body.p: Two cautions for low go-arounds. The airplane cannot climb below minimum power required speed, so the nose may need to come down briefly to gain airspeed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. And near the ground the cushion of ground effect is borrowed performance; climbing out of it too soon can leave the airplane unable to climb or even hold altitude at full power [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

**Failure to promptly initiate a missed approach.** What you see: at the MAP the learner keeps flying level, says "let me check," reaches for the GPS, or adds power slowly. The AFH lists indecision, delay, late or abrupt power and failure to configure among go-around errors [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. The cause is usually landing expectancy or an unbriefed missed. The fix: one word, "Missed," and the hands move: power, attitude, then clean up. Build the flow in a simulator first, where practice can continue until the task is done well [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

callout.text: Power, attitude, configuration; then navigate, then talk [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[23:312|IFH 10-21]].

check.q: Your learner adds full power at the MAP and immediately raises all the flaps. What can happen, and what do you teach?
check.a: A sudden, complete flap retraction can cause a loss of lift and settling. Stop the descent first, then raise the flaps in small steps as recommended, letting the airplane accelerate [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

chunks.title: Positive aircraft control in the climb

body.p: **Importance of positive aircraft control.** Airplane control is the first consideration in this high-workload phase [[24:182|AFH 9-11]], and positive aircraft control is the first special emphasis area on the checkride (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). The learner has to fly by instruments while turning, talking and reading the chart.

head: Phase
Instruments and technique to teach
rows: Climb entry from a slow speed
Raise the miniature aircraft to the climb attitude for the climb speed while power goes up to the climb setting; the VSI trends up and then steadies [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]
Stabilized climb
At constant airspeed the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch and the heading indicator for bank; tachometer or manifold pressure for power [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]
Level-off at the missed approach altitude
Lead by about 10 percent of the vertical speed: 500 fpm, 50 ft [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]
Partial panel
Climb entries are easier and more accurate from climbing speed [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]; with limited instruments use only small, precise inputs, because rapid ones cause oscillation [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]

body.p: **Brief the illusions.** A rapid acceleration stimulates the otolith organs like tilting the head back and can create the somatogravic illusion of a nose-up attitude, especially without good visual references; the disoriented pilot may push into a nose-low or dive attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. An abrupt change from climb to level flight can create the inversion illusion of tumbling backwards, with an abrupt push to a nose-low attitude [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5b2(e)]]. Only visual reference to fixed points on the ground or to the flight instruments prevents disorientation from these illusions [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5b1]]. Application: full power at low airspeed in cloud is a rapid acceleration too, so teach the learner to hold the pitch on the attitude indicator, not the one the body feels.

**Faulty basic instrument flying technique.** On the missed it looks like a pitch that wanders as airspeed changes, a VSI chased up and down, no trim, an overshoot of the missed approach altitude, or heading drift while the learner reads the chart. The IFH names the causes: not varying the cross-check during attitude and power changes, not holding the new pitch attitude, not trimming, not cross-checking airspeed and vertical speed before a correction, chasing the VSI, and not noting the climb rate to set the level-off lead [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. The fix is a faster cross-check during the change, trim, and small corrections. Application: on the ground, have the learner name the primary instruments for each phase in the table before flying it.

callout.text: If you must take over on a low missed, take the controls and calmly say "I have the flight controls." There is nothing to gain from fighting an anxious learner for control [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: Climbing on the missed in cloud, your learner says, "We're pitched up too steeply," and pushes forward, although the attitude indicator showed the briefed climb attitude. What happened, and what do you teach?
check.a: Probably the somatogravic illusion from the acceleration, which feels like a nose-up attitude and leads pilots to push nose-low [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Hold the attitude indicator's picture; only the flight instruments prevent disorientation without outside references [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5b1]].

body.p: **Performance of recommended checklist items appropriate to the go-around procedure.** The recommended items come from the airplane's AFM or POH; the AFH's flap and gear order applies unless the AFM/POH says otherwise [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. The PTS evaluates checklist use throughout; when reading a checklist during the maneuver would be unsafe or impracticable for a single pilot, review it after the elements are done (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).

bullets: Power full or maximum allowable; carburetor heat off, as applicable [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Flaps up in steps as recommended; gear up after a positive rate of climb [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
Rough trim first, precise trim once conditions are stable [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

Altitude preselector: missed approach altitude set after glideslope capture, or once level at the MDA; with the MDA left in the window, accurate flight director guidance is not available for the missed [[29:176|IPH 4-36]] [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].
GPS: sequence a non-WAAS receiver past the MAWP after crossing it, with extra inputs when the first leg is a course [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(f)(1)]] [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(f)(2)]].
Autopilot: the AFM gives the procedures and limits for using it on an approach [[29:176|IPH 4-36]].

body.p: The IPH crew briefing shows a spoken flow: "go-around thrust, flaps 15, positive climb, gear up, set me up" [[29:182|IPH 4-42]]. A briefing can also serve as a checklist that everything is set up correctly [[29:182|IPH 4-42]]. Application: build a single-pilot version for the training airplane from its POH, say it aloud as a flow, then confirm it with the printed checklist when climbing and stable.

callout.text: Application: in the learner tells, instructor does step, have the learner call the go-around flow while you fly it, so a misunderstanding is corrected before the learner is absorbed in controlling the airplane [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Level at the MDA, your learner's autopilot still shows the MDA in the altitude window. Why does that matter for the missed?
check.a: With the MDA left in the window, accurate flight director guidance is not available for the missed approach; set the missed approach altitude once level at the MDA [[29:176|IPH 4-36]] [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

body.p: **Required report to ATC.** When a landing cannot be made, advise ATC [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21a]]. The pilot tells ATC a missed approach will be made and why, unless ATC started it [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a2]], then requests clearance for a specific action: another approach, holding for improved conditions, or an alternate airport [[34:5|AIM 5-5-5a6]] [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21f]]. "When approach has been missed" is one of the reports made without an ATC request [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(d)]].

head: Report
IPH example
rows: Missed approach
"Marathon 564, missed approach, request clearance to Chicago." [[29:105|IPH Figure 2-68]]
Unable to climb at least 500 fpm
"Marathon 564, maximum climb rate 400 feet per minute." [[29:105|IPH Figure 2-68]]
Reaching a holding fix: time and altitude
"Marathon 564, FARGO Intersection at 05, 10,000, holding east." [[29:105|IPH Figure 2-68]]
Leaving a holding fix
"Marathon 564, leaving FARGO Intersection." [[29:105|IPH Figure 2-68]]
Loss of nav or comm capability (91.187)
"Marathon 564, ILS receiver inoperative." [[29:105|IPH Figure 2-68]]

body.p: If equipment caused the missed, 14 CFR 91.187 requires the pilot under IFR in controlled airspace to report a navigation, approach or communication malfunction as soon as practical, with the aircraft identification, the equipment affected, how much the IFR capability is impaired and the help wanted from ATC [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(a)]] [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(b)]].

At an airport without an operating control tower, continuous contact with ATC may not be possible: fly the go-around or missed approach without delay and contact ATC when able [[33:453|AIM 5-4-21h]]. On a practice approach there, also announce on the CTAF when executing the missed approach [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g6]].

**Failure to make the required report to ATC.** What you hear: nothing, a call only after the controller asks, or "going around" with no request. Cause: overload and no plan for what to ask for. Fix: fly first, but then make the call: "missed approach," the reason, the request. Application: make the request a decision on the ground: try again, hold, or divert.

check.q: On the missed at a non-towered field, your learner cannot reach Center below 2,000 ft. What should the learner do?
check.a: Fly the missed approach without delay and contact ATC when able, because continuous contact may not be possible there [[33:453|AIM 5-4-21h]].

chunks.title: Flying the published or alternate missed approach

body.p: **Compliance with the published or alternate missed approach procedure.** An approach clearance includes the published missed approach unless ATC says otherwise [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]]. From the MAP the pilot flies the missed approach for the procedure being used, or an alternate one specified by ATC [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21a]] [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a3]].

head: Case
What the learner does
rows: Published missed
Fly it from the MAP; it protects only on the missed approach segment from or above the MAP, with a climb of 200 ft/NM or more as published [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]]
Radar vectors

Where radar service is provided, follow vectors given in place of the published missed [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21d]]; controllers may vector a radar-identified airplane on a missed approach [[34:5|AIM 5-5-5b2]]
Alternate missed from ATC
Issued, for example, when the primary missed approach NAVAID fails during the approach [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21e]] [[34:5|AIM 5-5-5b1]]
Alternate missed by NOTAM
A mandatory part of the procedure; the text is not on the chart, but its holding pattern is [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21e]], in an inset [[2:115|Chart Users' Guide p 115]]
Holding at the missed approach fix
Fly the track and pattern on the plan view [[23:42|IFH 1-23]]; more climb may be needed in the hold before going back to the IAF or to an alternate [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21g]]
Leaving the published missed
Only after climbing to a safe altitude, especially without radar; leaving early may not give terrain clearance [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21g]]

body.p: Holding entries, speeds and timing are taught in lesson FII.VII.B.

**Failure to comply with the missed approach procedure.** Typical forms: turning before the MAP, climbing straight ahead when the procedure says turn, stopping short of the published altitude, skipping the climb-in-hold, flying an extended final because a non-WAAS GPS was not sequenced [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(f)(1)]], or cutting toward the next approach before reaching a safe altitude [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21g]]. Causes: no briefing, automation surprises, haste. Fix: brief the first two steps, say the turn direction and altitude aloud at the MAP, and check the track on the map. An early turn matters most, because the protected airspace makes no allowance for an abnormally early turn [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]].

callout.text: A missed started away from the MAP, from below the MDA or DA(H), or on a circling approach does not necessarily get obstacle clearance from the published missed, and separation from other traffic is not assured [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]].

check.q: Climbing on the missed, below the published altitude, your learner asks for "direct to the IAF to try again" in a nonradar area. What do you teach?
check.a: Climb to a safe altitude before proceeding off the published missed, especially without radar; abandoning it early may not give adequate terrain clearance [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21g]].

chunks.title: Climb gradients: plan the climb before the approach

body.p: Missed approach obstacle protection assumes at least 200 ft per NM unless a higher gradient is published in the chart notes; a higher gradient ends at a stated altitude or fix [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. Obstacles or terrain in the missed approach segment are why a steeper gradient is required [[29:181|IPH 4-41]]. Pilots must preplan that the airplane can meet the gradient, in feet per NM, and remember that flying faster over the ground than planned raises the climb rate needed in feet per minute [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]].

**From ft/NM to fpm.** The TPP booklets carry a conversion table on page D1 [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. In the IPH example, 297 ft/NM at 180 knots groundspeed needs 892 fpm [[29:34|IPH Figure 1-17]]. Read across the same row and the rate grows with groundspeed: 297 ft/NM needs 297 fpm at 60 knots, 446 at 90 and 595 at 120 [[29:34|IPH Figure 1-17]].
The gradient is also height per distance. In the IFH departure example, the standard 200 ft/NM puts an airplane 400 ft above the ground 2 NM from the departure end of the runway [[23:61|IFH 2-10]].

**Speed and category.** Category protection includes the missed approach climb surface and turn containment at the category's speeds, so a faster approach can require a higher category's minimums [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].

callout.text: Teach the trap: a learner checks the gradient at the planned groundspeed and then flies the missed with a tailwind. The gradient is the same, but the climb rate needed goes up with groundspeed [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. Application: check the POH climb chart for the day's weight and density altitude; no source here gives your airplane's numbers.

check.q: The missed needs 318 ft/NM and you expect 120 knots groundspeed. What does the table give, and why does groundspeed matter?
check.a: 637 fpm in the 3.0° row at 120 knots; at 90 knots the same gradient needs 478 fpm [[29:34|IPH Figure 1-17]]. A higher groundspeed raises the fpm needed for the same gradient [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]].

body.p: **Notification of ATC if the aircraft is unable to comply with a clearance, instruction, restriction, or climb gradient.** A clearance never authorizes deviating from a rule, regulation or minimum altitude, or unsafe operation; if a clearance would put the aircraft in jeopardy, the pilot must request an amended clearance [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1a]] [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1b]]. The pilot asks for clarification or amendment whenever a clearance is not fully understood or is unacceptable for safety, and when a deviation is necessary, advises ATC as soon as possible and gets an amended clearance [[34:2|AIM 5-5-2a3]] [[34:2|AIM 5-5-2a4]]. When uncertain of a clearance, ask ATC immediately [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]].

Before the approach: choose minimums or a procedure that need no steeper climb [[29:181|IPH 4-41]]. In the climb: report when unable to climb at least 500 fpm [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(c)]]
An alternate missed, issued after starting the approach, that needs equipment the approach did not
May reject it [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21e]]

The PIC may deviate [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]], and must notify ATC as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]]

body.p: **Teach the words.** The IPH example for a slow climb is "Marathon 564, maximum climb rate 400 feet per minute" [[29:105|IPH Figure 2-68]], and the report is expected without an ATC request [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(c)]]. Application: a learner in a low-powered trainer on a hot day should have that call ready before the approach.

callout.text: Application: in the simulator, play a controller who issues a missed approach altitude, speed or route the airplane cannot meet. The learner should say "unable," give what the airplane can do, and ask for an alternative.

check.q: Climbing out of Daggett on a hot afternoon, your learner sees 350 fpm on the VSI. Besides flying the airplane, what should the learner tell ATC?
check.a: That the airplane cannot climb at least 500 fpm, for example by giving the maximum climb rate [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(c)]] [[29:105|IPH Figure 2-68]]. Whether 350 fpm still meets 220 ft per NM depends on groundspeed, which is why it is planned before the approach [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]].

chunks.title: Going missed early, and not below the MDA

body.p: A pilot may start the missed before the MAP, but the protected airspace has buffers for normal maneuvers and no allowance for an abnormally early turn. So unless ATC clears otherwise, fly the approach as charted to the MAP at or above the MDA or DH before turning [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]] [[23:40|IFH 1-21]] [[23:312|IFH 10-21]].

bullets: **Lateral:** fly the lateral path of the procedure to the MAP [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a4]].

**Vertical:** climb to the missed approach altitude, except when a maximum altitude is specified between the FAF and the MAP; then comply with the maximum, which may mean continuing to descend on final [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a4]].

**Non-WAAS GPS:** activating the missed before the MAWP switches the CDI to ±1 NM at once, but the receiver keeps navigating to the MAWP and will not sequence past it; do not turn before the MAWP [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(f)(1)]].
**WAAS:** the missed may be selected before the MAWP, but navigation continues to the MAWP before sequencing [[33:106|AIM 1-1-18d7]].

body.p: **The Orlando example.** On the Orlando Executive ILS or LOC RWY 7, the altitude at BUVAY (ORL 3 DME) is restricted to keep aircraft out of the overlying protected airspace for approach routes into Orlando International, so on a missed started before BUVAY a pilot may have to continue down to 1,200 ft before going on to the MAP [[29:181|IPH 4-41]]. The chart note says so, and the missed is a climb to 1200 maximum to SOTCO, then a climbing left turn to 1500 to OVIDO and hold [[29:184|IPH Figure 4-23]].

**Descent below the MDA prior to initiating a missed approach.** What you see: the learner has given up on the approach but first takes a look below the MDA, or sags below it while deciding, and then goes missed. It breaks 91.175(c) [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(c)]] and throws away the protection, which assumes the missed starts at the MAP not lower than the MDA [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]; from below the MDA, the published missed does not necessarily give obstacle clearance [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]]. Cause: landing expectancy [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] and loose altitude control while looking outside. Fix: the MDA is a floor until 91.175(c) is met; decide at the MAP and go. Contrast a DA, as lesson FII.VIII.A does: the missed starts at the DA, obstacle clearance allows a momentary descent below it during the transition to the missed, and the airplane continues along the final approach course to at least the runway threshold waypoint or MAP before any turn [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m5(a)]]. An MDA allows no such dip. Application: teach it with callouts at the MDA and at the MAP.

callout.text: Application: on an early missed, have the learner say the plan aloud: "Missed now, track to the MAP, climb to (or hold) the published altitude, turn at the MAP." On a non-WAAS GPS the needle still points to the MAWP, which supports that plan.

check.q: On the Orlando LOC RWY 7, your learner goes missed before BUVAY at 1,600 ft and climbs straight ahead toward 2,000. What do you teach?
check.a: The missed is a climb to 1200 maximum, and the note warns that a descent to 1200 may be required on an early missed [[29:184|IPH Figure 4-23]]. Fly the localizer to the MAP while complying with the maximum altitude, even if it means continuing down [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a4]].

body.p: If visual reference is lost while circling to land, follow the missed approach for that procedure unless ATC specifies an alternate. Make an initial climbing turn toward the landing runway and keep turning until established on the missed approach course [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]]. The IFH says the same: climbing turn toward the landing runway, then intercept and fly the missed approach course [[23:312|IFH 10-21]].

The circle may be flown in more than one direction, so the path to the missed approach course depends on where the airplane is when visual reference is lost. Following the procedure helps keep it laterally within the circling and missed approach obstruction clearance areas [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21c]]. In FIG 5-4-30, each decision to miss is followed by a climbing turn toward the runways, whichever side the airplane was on [[33:452|AIM 5-4-21c]].

When it applies: at or above the MDA while circling, the missed is required whenever an identifiable part of the airport is not distinctly visible, unless only a normal bank hides it [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]]. Straight-in nonprecision and circling procedures share the same MAP [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f5]]. Vertically, a missed started on a circling approach does not necessarily get obstacle clearance from the published missed [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]].

**Balked landing past the MAP.** Contact ATC as soon as possible for an amended clearance; if unable, try to re-intercept a published segment of the missed and follow its route and altitudes; if that is no longer appropriate, consider staying visual to land again, or a circle-climb over the airport [[33:452|AIM 5-4-21h]] [[33:453|AIM 5-4-21h]]. Before the approach the pilot should already have weighed the weather, performance, charted obstacles, the departure procedure and other traffic for that case [[33:453|AIM 5-4-21h]].

callout.text: Following the procedure, with its initial climbing turn toward the landing runway, helps keep the airplane inside the circling and missed approach protected areas [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21c]]; a learner who turns away toward the published missed course has not followed it. Application: before the circle, have the learner say which way any miss will turn from each leg. Task D covers the circling maneuver itself.

check.q: Circling in left traffic, your learner loses the airport in a cloud on the downwind and starts a climbing right turn toward the published missed course. What do you say?
check.a: Turn the other way: a climbing left turn toward the landing runway, continued until established on the missed approach course [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]]. Turning away can take the airplane outside the protected areas [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21c]].

chunks.title: The MFD, GPS and autopilot on the missed

body.p: **Uses of the MFD and other graphical navigational displays, if installed, to monitor position and track to help navigate the missed approach.** An MFD can show a moving map, approach charts, terrain awareness and weather [[23:123|IFH 5-28]]. Moving maps improve situational awareness with a picture of the airplane's position relative to NAVAIDs, waypoints, airspace, terrain and hazardous weather [[23:29|IFH 1-10]] [[23:30|IFH 1-11]]. A GPS shows track, bearing, groundspeed and distance; with track and bearing matched by the right heading, the airplane goes directly to the waypoint [[23:272|IFH 9-29]].

What the display helps the learner check
rows: At the MAP
Groundspeed, which sets the climb rate the gradient needs [[23:272|IFH 9-29]] [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]
First turn
The direction, and that it does not start before the MAP or MAWP [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]] [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(f)(1)]]
Non-WAAS GPS
Sequencing: if not sequenced it shows an extension of the final course and the distance from the MAWP keeps growing [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(f)(1)]]

Automatic sequencing past the MAWP when the missed was designed for RNAV [[33:106|AIM 1-1-18d7]]; CDI scaling changes abruptly to missed approach scaling near the departure end or when the pilot selects it [[33:106|AIM 1-1-18d5]]
Conventional missed
A suitable RNAV system may navigate to or from a VOR or NDB or hold over one, but not fly localizer courses without raw localizer data [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3c]]

body.p: **Teach the limits.** The IFH calls the electronic flight display a supplementary source of navigation data that does not replace the charts; the pilot follows the flight on the chart while monitoring the display, which matters most if the display fails [[23:329|IFH 11-4]]. With the autopilot, use anticipate, act, verify: know what should happen, push the button, then check that the airplane does it [[30:51|RMH 7-2]]. A change of navigation source can drop the autopilot to a lower mode such as wings level [[30:52|RMH 7-3]]. One of the most common errors is not moving to a lower level of automation as things change; when automation surprises the learner, reduce the level, fly by hand and fix it later [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

callout.text: Application: on a practice missed, ask "Show me where we go next." The learner points to the next fix on the map and on the chart and says the heading that keeps track and bearing together. That builds the map into the scan instead of replacing it.

check.q: Past the MAWP on a non-WAAS GPS, the map shows the airplane on an extended final with the distance growing. What happened, and what do you teach?
check.a: The missed approach was not activated; the receiver will not sequence past the MAWP until the pilot does it, and a course leg needs extra inputs [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(f)(1)]] [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(f)(2)]]. Teach that receiver's exact steps before IMC.

chunks.title: Demonstrate and explain the missed approach

body.p: **Demonstrates and simultaneously explains a missed approach from an instructional standpoint.** The explanation during the demonstration must be clear, concise, technically accurate and complete with no prompting, while you fly to the instrument pilot skill level (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). In the demonstration phase the instructor may describe the actions while doing them, and any deviation from the explanation should be acknowledged and explained at once [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Demonstrate in the same order as the explanation, exactly as the learner should practice it, safety procedures included [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
**A talk-through you can use** (add your POH power, pitch and flap settings):

bullets: "Briefed: at the MAP without the runway, climb to ___, then ___ to ___ and hold. Missed approach altitude is set [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]."
"MAP, no listed reference: missed approach. Full power, carb heat off [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]."
"Climb attitude on the attitude indicator; forward pressure and right rudder against the pitch-up and left yaw; rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]."
"Descent stopped: flaps up one step, accelerating [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Positive rate of climb: gear up, if retractable [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]."
"At the MAP, turning as published, not before [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. GPS sequenced past the MAWP [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(f)(1)]]."
"Center, (call sign), missed approach, (reason), request (another approach, hold or the alternate) [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a2]] [[34:5|AIM 5-5-5a6]]."
"Climbing at 500 fpm, I start the level-off 50 ft early [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. Now I review the go-around checklist."

body.p: Then hand it over in steps. In learner tells, instructor does, the learner talks you through it, so misunderstandings are fixed before the learner is busy flying. In learner tells, learner does, the learner thinks aloud, so you can tell a misconception from a motor-skill error [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

callout.text: Positive exchange of flight controls: "You have the flight controls." "I have the flight controls." "You have the flight controls." Brief it before flight and add a visual check [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: During your demonstration you start the published turn a few seconds before the MAP while explaining. What should you do?
check.a: Acknowledge and explain the deviation at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. No allowance is made for an abnormally early turn, so the turn waits for the MAP [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]].

body.p: **Analyzes and corrects simulated common errors related to a missed approach.** The evaluator acts as a learner and flies the errors on purpose; the listed errors may or may not be in the references, and the evaluator will not simulate any condition that may jeopardize safe flight (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). Name the error, say what the instruments show, give the likely cause and the fix, and say how you would teach it.

body.p: **Simulating it safely.** Brief the view-limiting device, when and how it goes on and off, before flight (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction), and the positive exchange of flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Tell ATC how each practice approach will end, such as a missed or low approach [[33:264|AIM 4-3-22b]]; a VFR aircraft practicing approaches is not automatically authorized to fly the missed and must request it [[33:265|AIM 4-3-22e]]. The safety pilot needs at least the right pilot certificate and adequate vision forward and to each side [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]].

Safety permitting, let a learner go partway into a mistake and find the way out, since learners seldom learn a maneuver well without correcting errors [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]; but learners must never exceed your limits [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. To test understanding, vary the missed or combine it with a hold or a diversion; a learner who memorized one will struggle [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

callout.text: Application: in the airplane, "partway into the mistake" never includes an early turn near terrain or a descent below the MDA or DA. Simulate "no runway" by keeping the device on at the MAP; practice balked landings and circling misses in a simulator, or in VMC at a height you briefed.

check.q: The examiner, acting as your learner, reaches the MAP, says "missed," then flies level for five seconds working the GPS. Name the error and the fix.
check.a: Failure to promptly initiate the missed approach; indecision and delay are listed go-around errors [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Power and climb attitude first, configuration next; the GPS waits until the airplane is climbing [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

scenario.title: LPV practice at Daggett on a hot afternoon
scenario.setup: You are a new CFII. Your instrument learner, about 30 hours into training, flies a WAAS-equipped, fixed-gear single in Category A. You are on an IFR flight plan in good VMC for practice approaches at Daggett, a non-towered airport (Figure 4-26). The learner is under a view-limiting device; you are instructor and safety pilot. It is a hot afternoon, and the learner wants the RNAV (GPS) RWY 26 to the LPV DA # line, then the published missed approach.

questions.q: What must the learner check before choosing the 2217 line?
questions.a: That the airplane can climb at least 220 ft per NM to 8000; pilots must preplan it, and a higher groundspeed raises the climb rate needed [[29:187|IPH Figure 4-26]] [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. If the POH climb data for today's weight and density altitude say no, use the LPV DA line at 2438, which needs no steeper climb [[29:181|IPH 4-41]].

questions.q: What do you brief and coordinate about the practice approach?
questions.a: How and when the device goes on and off (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction), the positive exchange of flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]], and how the approach will end: tell ATC a missed approach is planned [[33:264|AIM 4-3-22b]]. On the CTAF, announce the approach and when the missed is executed [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g6]].

questions.q: At 2217 ft, with the device still on, the learner says, "The GPS shows 0.8 miles to go; I'll hold it level a bit." What do you say?
questions.a: Missed approach now. On LPV the missed starts at the DA without the references and must not wait for the distance to reach zero [[33:106|AIM 1-1-18d7]] [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]].

questions.q: In the climb the learner pulls the nose up hard as the power comes in, and the airspeed falls. What do you teach?
questions.a: Hold forward pressure and right rudder against the power's pitch-up and left yaw, set the climb attitude, and rough trim; a nose that rises too early can cause a stall when low [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Improper pitch attitude is a listed go-around error [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

questions.q: Climbing at 350 fpm, the learner cannot raise Center at this altitude. What should the learner do?
questions.a: Keep flying the published missed without delay and call when able; continuous contact may not be possible at a non-towered field [[33:453|AIM 5-4-21h]]. Once in contact: missed approach, the reason and the request [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a2]], plus the report of being unable to climb at least 500 fpm [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(c)]].

questions.q: The airplane reaches NULMN at 7,000 ft. What does the procedure require, and how do you debrief the flight?
questions.a: Enter the hold and continue the climb in the hold to 8000 [[29:187|IPH Figure 4-26]], and report the time and altitude on reaching the holding fix [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(f)]]. Debrief with the learner's self-assessment first, then your assessment and a comparison of the two [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

skills.do: Demonstrate a missed approach at the MAP or DA while explaining the decision, power, climb attitude, flaps and gear, the published or ATC missed, the report and request to ATC, and the checklist review, at instrument pilot standards; explain how an early missed and a circling miss differ.
skills.practice: Fly the talk-through aloud in a simulator first, then in the airplane [[25:174|AIH 9-4]], in the same order every time you explain it [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. In the airplane, have a qualified safety pilot aboard [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]] and another applicant play ATC.

skills.do: As the evaluator flies the K2 errors (chart knowledge, missed conditions, late initiation, no ATC report, not following the procedure, faulty technique, descent below the MDA), name each one, say what the instruments show, give the cause and the fix, and say how you would teach it.
skills.practice: Take turns with another applicant flying the errors in the table and correcting them by thinking aloud, so you can tell misconceptions from motor-skill errors [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]; vary the approach to test understanding [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

quiz.q: Your learner briefs the missed approach from the profile icons only. What is the problem?
options: Only the first four may be shown, so steps can be missing
The icons are advisory and may be ignored in IMC
The icons apply only to the precision line of minima
The icons show the alternate missed, not the published one
quiz.why: When space is short only the first four icon boxes are shown, so the icons may not represent the whole procedure; the complete text is in the middle briefing strip [[2:115|Chart Users' Guide p 115]] [[33:419|AIM 5-4-5m7(c)]]. They are not limited to precision lines, and alternate missed approach text is not on the chart at all [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21e]].

quiz.q: At the MAP of a VOR approach your learner sees the REIL, has the published flight visibility and can make a normal descent. What now?
options: Go missed; the runway itself must be seen
Continue; REIL is a listed visual reference
Level at the MDA until the threshold shows
Go missed; REIL counts only with a glidepath
quiz.why: Runway end identifier lights are one of the listed references, and with the visibility and a normal descent all three 91.175(c) conditions are met [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(v)]] [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]]. The rule does not require the runway itself or a glidepath.

quiz.q: Circling at the MDA, your learner loses sight of the airport for a moment only because of the bank in the turn to base. What does 91.175(e)(2) require?
options: An immediate missed approach
A climb back up to the FAF altitude
No missed approach for that alone
A report to ATC before continuing
quiz.why: The missed is required when an identifiable part of the airport is not distinctly visible while circling, unless the loss results only from a normal bank [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]]. If the airport stays out of sight for any other reason, the missed is required at once.

quiz.q: At the MAP your learner applies full power. Per the AFH's three principles, what comes next?
options: Raising the flaps
Calling ATC with a request
Raising the landing gear
Climb pitch attitude
quiz.why: The order is power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Flaps come up after the descent is stopped and the gear after a positive rate of climb [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]; ATC is advised after the airplane is configured and turning [[23:312|IFH 10-21]].

quiz.q: On a low missed your learner raises all the flaps at once right after adding power. What can happen?
options: The engine may falter under the sudden load
The airplane may settle from lost lift
Nothing, since the power is already full
The stall warning may stop working
quiz.why: A sudden and complete flap retraction can cause a loss of lift and settling into the ground; raise them in small steps [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Engine faltering is linked to abrupt throttle movement, not flap retraction [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

quiz.q: Climbing on the missed in cloud, your learner feels the nose is too high and pushes forward, although the attitude indicator is correct. Which illusion is likely?
options: Somatogravic
Coriolis
Graveyard spiral
Autokinesis
quiz.why: A rapid acceleration creates the somatogravic illusion of a nose-up attitude, and the pilot may push into a nose-low attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Coriolis comes from head movement in a prolonged turn, and autokinesis from staring at a light in the dark [[23:73|IFH 3-6]] [[23:74|IFH 3-7]].

quiz.q: The missed needs 297 ft/NM and your learner expects 120 knots groundspeed. Using the table, what climb rate is needed?
options: 446 fpm
892 fpm
595 fpm
quiz.why: In the 2.8° row (297 ft/NM), the 120-knot column reads 595 fpm [[29:34|IPH Figure 1-17]]. 446 fpm is the 90-knot value; using it at 120 knots would leave the airplane below the gradient, since a higher groundspeed needs a higher rate [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]].

quiz.q: Two miles before the MAP on a VOR approach your learner decides to go missed. The missed starts with a climbing right turn. When may the learner turn?
options: Right away, toward the holding fix
At the MAP, unless ATC says otherwise
After climbing 500 ft straight ahead
Once the published altitude is reached
quiz.why: No consideration is given to an abnormally early turn, so fly the procedure to the MAP at or above the MDA before turning, unless ATC clears otherwise [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]] [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]. Neither a height gain nor the missed approach altitude makes an early turn protected.

quiz.q: On the Orlando LOC RWY 7 your learner goes missed before BUVAY at 1,600 ft. What does the procedure call for?
options: Climb to 1500 and turn left toward OVIDO
Hold 1,600 until the MAP, then climb
Climb to the 3000 MSA, then turn
Descend to 1200 maximum, then on to the MAP
quiz.why: The missed is a climb to 1200 maximum, and the note says a descent to 1200 may be required on an early missed [[29:184|IPH Figure 4-23]]. On an early missed, comply with a maximum altitude between the FAF and MAP, even if that means continued descent [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a4]]. The left turn to 1500 starts at SOTCO, after the MAP.

quiz.q: Circling in left traffic, your learner loses the airport on the downwind. Which way should the initial turn go?
options: Right, toward the published missed approach course
Straight ahead until reaching the MAP
Left, climbing toward the landing runway
Either way, as long as it is a climb
quiz.why: Make an initial climbing turn toward the landing runway and continue until established on the missed approach course [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]]. In left traffic the runway is on the left. Turning away can leave the protected areas [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21c]].

quiz.q: Your learner chose to go missed. What should the first call to ATC contain?
options: Missed approach, the reason, a request
Only the altitude now being climbed to
Nothing until reaching the missed approach holding fix
A request for a contact approach
quiz.why: Advise ATC of the missed approach and the reason, unless ATC started it [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a2]], and request clearance for a specific action [[34:5|AIM 5-5-5a6]]. The holding fix report of time and altitude comes later [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(f)]].

quiz.q: Past the MAWP, the non-WAAS GPS shows an extended final with growing distance. Why?
options: RAIM was lost after the FAWP
The CDI changed to ±1 NM
The database expired during the flight
The receiver was not sequenced
quiz.why: If the missed is not activated, the receiver shows an extension of the final course and the distance from the MAWP grows until it is manually sequenced [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(f)(1)]]. The ±1 NM change happens when the missed is activated before the MAWP.

quiz.q: On a low go-around your learner freezes at idle power. What does the AIH say about taking control?
options: Wait, so the learner finds the way out
Talk the learner through it, hands off
Take control, saying "I have the flight controls"
Share the controls so the learner keeps the feel
quiz.why: When necessary, take the controls and calmly announce "I have the flight controls"; a learner left on the controls can keep the instructor from full and effective control [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Letting a learner go partway into a mistake applies only when safety permits [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the Daggett RNAV (GPS) RWY 26 have two LPV lines?
options: One is for WAAS and one is for baro-VNAV
The lower DA needs a 220 ft/NM missed climb
The higher DA is for night operations only
One line is for the Victorville altimeter
final_quiz.why: When the missed needs more than 200 ft/NM, a newer standard publishes two sets: the lower requires the steeper climb, the higher does not [[29:181|IPH 4-41]]. The # on the 2217 line points to the note requiring 220 ft per NM to 8000 [[29:187|IPH Figure 4-26]]. The Victorville setting raises minimums through a note, not a separate LPV line.

final_quiz.q: A missed needs 370 ft/NM. Your learner planned 90 knots groundspeed, but a tailwind makes it 120 knots. What rate does the table give now?
options: 555 fpm
745 fpm
370 fpm
final_quiz.why: The 3.5° row (370 ft/NM) reads 555 fpm at 90 knots and 745 fpm at 120 knots [[29:34|IPH Figure 1-17]]. A higher groundspeed than planned raises the climb rate needed [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]], so 555 fpm would fall short.

final_quiz.q: Which statement about the standard missed approach climb is correct?
options: 200 ft/NM, unless the notes publish a higher gradient
200 fpm, at whatever groundspeed is flown
Required on precision approaches only
Advisory only for single-engine airplanes
final_quiz.why: A climb gradient of at least 200 ft per NM is required unless a higher one is published in the notes [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. It is a gradient per NM, not a rate per minute, and it is not limited to precision approaches.

final_quiz.q: After your learner begins the approach, ATC issues an alternate missed that needs DME, which the approach did not need and the airplane lacks. What may the learner do?
options: Accept it, since it is a clearance
Fly it with estimated DME distances
Fly the published missed and say nothing
Reject it
final_quiz.why: Pilots may reject an alternate missed requiring equipment not needed for the published approach when it is issued after beginning the approach [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21e]]. Flying the published missed without telling ATC would deviate from a clearance without an amendment [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]].

final_quiz.q: An alternate missed approach is put in effect by NOTAM. What is its status?
options: Advisory; the chart still governs
Used only if ATC repeats it
For radar-equipped aircraft only
Mandatory part of the procedure
final_quiz.why: When implemented by NOTAM, the alternate missed becomes a mandatory part of the procedure, and the NOTAM gives the text and any extra equipment [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21e]]. Its holding pattern is shown in an inset, but its text is not on the chart [[2:115|Chart Users' Guide p 115]].

final_quiz.q: In a nonradar area, your learner wants to leave the missed for a shortcut to the IAF before reaching the published altitude. What do you teach?
options: Leave it now, since the IAF is closer
Leave it once safely above the MDA
Climb to a safe altitude first
Leave it after the first published turn
final_quiz.why: Make sure the airplane has climbed to a safe altitude before proceeding off the published missed, especially in nonradar areas; abandoning it before the published altitude may not give terrain clearance [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21g]]. Being above the MDA is not the same as a safe altitude.

final_quiz.q: On a practice approach at a non-towered airport, when does the AIM say to announce on the CTAF, among other times?
options: Upon executing the missed approach
Only on a short final
Only when leaving the hold
When filing the flight plan
final_quiz.why: Announce departing the FAF inbound, established on final or when released by ATC, on completion or termination, and upon executing the missed approach [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g6]]. Leaving a holding fix is an ATC report [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(g)]].

final_quiz.q: Under IFR in controlled airspace, the ILS receiver fails during the approach and your learner goes missed. What does 14 CFR 91.187 require?
options: A written report to the FAA within 48 hours
A report to ATC as soon as practical
Squawk 7600 until on the ground
Nothing if a GPS still works
final_quiz.why: Report in-flight malfunctions of navigation, approach or communication equipment to ATC as soon as practical, with the identification, equipment, impairment and help wanted [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(a)]] [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(b)]]. The 48-hour detailed report applies to a pilot given emergency priority, and only if ATC requests it [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]].

final_quiz.q: After a balked landing below the MDA, your learner cannot reach ATC. What does the AIM suggest?
options: Climb straight ahead to the MSA and hold
Squawk 7700 and circle at the MDA
Re-intercept a published missed segment
Turn toward the IAF for another approach
final_quiz.why: If unable to contact ATC, try to re-intercept a published segment of the missed and comply with its route and altitudes; if that is no longer appropriate, consider staying visual or a circle-climb over the airport [[33:452|AIM 5-4-21h]] [[33:453|AIM 5-4-21h]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner climbs at 500 fpm toward a 2,000 ft missed approach altitude. Using the IFH rule, when should the level-off start?
options: About 100 ft early
About 50 ft early
About 10 ft early
Right at 2,000 ft
final_quiz.why: Lead the level-off by about 10 percent of the vertical speed: 500 fpm, 50 ft [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. A 100 ft lead fits 1,000 fpm. Not noting the rate to set the lead is a listed error [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

final_quiz.q: On a WAAS LPV approach, when does the missed begin if the references are not in sight?
options: When the distance reads zero
At the MAWP at the threshold
100 ft below the DA
At the DA
final_quiz.why: On LPV and LNAV/VNAV, the missed is based on reaching the DA without the required references and must not be delayed while waiting for the distance to reach zero [[33:106|AIM 1-1-18d7]]. These lines have no MAWP; the distance runs to a point normally at the threshold.

final_quiz.q: Why can flying faster than the category speed require higher-category minimums, even for the missed approach?
options: Category speeds set the missed climb surface and turn room
Faster airplanes only need a longer landing runway
The VDP moves closer to the runway at speed
ATC separates arrivals by approach category
final_quiz.why: Category protection includes height loss at the DA, the missed approach climb surface and turn containment at the higher category speeds, so a faster approach can require higher-category minimums [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].

final_quiz.q: Which statement about the go-around is correct, per the AFH?
options: It is dangerous only if delayed or done poorly
It is always dangerous when flown in IMC
It shows a poor approach flown by an unskilled pilot
It may start below the MDA to look for lights
final_quiz.why: The go-around is not inherently dangerous; it becomes dangerous only when delayed unduly or executed improperly, and the idea that it shows poor skill is a fallacy [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Going below the MDA without 91.175(c) is never allowed [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(c)]].

final_quiz.q: A single pilot finds reading the go-around checklist during the initiation impracticable. What is acceptable?
options: Reading every item before moving the throttle
Skipping the checklist, since it is memorized
Reviewing it after the items are done
Having ATC read the items over the radio
final_quiz.why: The PTS accepts a review of the checklist after the elements are done when reading it during the maneuver would be unsafe or impracticable, especially single pilot (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). Airplane control is the first consideration in this high-workload phase [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

final_quiz.q: At Daggett, what does the missed approach say about altitude in the NULMN hold?
options: Hold at 7600 ft, the 25 NM MSA
Keep climbing in the hold to 8000
Descend in the hold to 6100 ft
Hold at 3800 ft, the altitude at the FAF
final_quiz.why: The text ends "continue climb-in-hold to 8000" [[29:187|IPH Figure 4-26]]. 7600 is the MSA, and the descent to 6100 applies to the HEC holding pattern before an approach [[29:187|IPH Figure 4-26]].

takeaways: At the MAP or DA without 91.175(c), or when the airport is lost while circling, the missed is required at once.
Brief the full missed approach text before the approach; the icons may not show it all.
Power, attitude, configuration: flaps in steps, gear after a positive rate, and fly the attitude indicator, not the feeling.
Protection assumes a start at the MAP, not below the MDA or DA, at 200 ft/NM or the published gradient, with no early turn.
Early missed: fly to the MAP, obey any maximum altitude, then turn. Circling miss: climbing turn toward the landing runway.
Tell ATC: missed approach, reason, request; say unable when you cannot meet a climb, restriction or clearance.
Use the map to confirm the turn and track, sequence the GPS, and drop to a lower level of automation when it surprises you.
Demonstrate while explaining in the same order, then let the learner tell and do; simulate errors only where it is safe.
cfi_notes: IPH 4-41 says obstacle clearance "is not provided" by the published missed when it starts away from the MAP, below the MDA or DA, or on a circling approach [[29:181|IPH 4-41]]; the AIM says "not necessarily provided" [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]]. Teach the AIM wording; either way, do not count on it.
The IFH uses "MAP" for both the missed approach point and the missed approach procedure ("When a MAP is initiated ...") [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]. Have learners say "point" or "procedure."

Order of the first actions: the AFH lists power first, then attitude [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]; the IFH sets the climb pitch attitude while setting climb power [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]. Teach them as one smooth action, with configuration after.

IPH 4-41 says steeper-gradient notes give fpm examples, with climb gradients in future charting [[29:181|IPH 4-41]]; the current AIM uses ft/NM with the TPP page D1 table [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. The handbook charts and table here date from 2010 to 2011; work the same problems on current charts.

AIM 5-4-5m7(c) says only four or fewer missed approach icons can be shown [[33:419|AIM 5-4-5m7(c)]]; the current Chart Users' Guide shows them all when space permits and only the first four when it does not, and its examples show more than four [[2:115|Chart Users' Guide p 115]], as the Daggett chart does [[29:187|IPH Figure 4-26]]. Either way, only the briefing strip text is complete.
IFH 10-21 lists "VASI" as a visual reference [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]; the current rule says "visual glideslope indicator" [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(vi)]]. Use the rule's words.

IFH 1-23 says to use the "next higher" category's minimums when faster than the category [[23:42|IFH 1-23]]; the IPH says the category that fits the speed, which can be two categories up [[29:148|IPH 4-8]]. Teach the IPH, which also ties it to the missed approach climb surface and turns.

How it is tested: the evaluator selects Tasks A and B and combines them with C, D or E, and may ask for a landing or a missed approach at the end of each approach (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area VIII). The evaluator acts as a learner to simulate errors, causes a realistic distraction, and puts special emphasis on positive aircraft control, checklist usage and positive exchange of flight controls (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).

Examiners like to ask: what an approach clearance includes, the early missed (fly to the MAP), the circling miss turn, climb gradient and groundspeed, alternate missed approaches by ATC or NOTAM, GPS sequencing, and what to report.
gaps: Go-around power, pitch attitude, flap retraction steps and speeds, Vx and Vy, climb performance and the go-around checklist for a given airplane come from its AFM/POH, which is not in the sources.
No source here gives a single-pilot GA missed approach callout script; the IPH callouts are a multi-crew example, and the talk-through in this lesson is teaching advice.
The current TPP rate of climb table (page D1) and current charts are not in the sources; the IPH table and charts date from 2010 to 2011.
No source here says how to simulate "no runway in sight" or a lost circling reference in the airplane; the methods given are advice and must stay within the PTS rule that nothing unsafe is simulated.
The CFII PTS gives no numeric tolerances for this Task; the Instrument ACS tolerances (in lesson IR.VI.C) are not in the build sources.
Multiengine missed approaches with an engine inoperative (Tasks IX.C and IX.D) are left out of this course.

activities.title: Where is it on the chart?
activities.intro: Tap an item, then tap where you find it on an approach chart.

pairs.r: Middle briefing strip, missed approach box
Upper corner of the profile box
Hatched line with an arrow in the plan view

pairs.l: Time from the FAF to the MAP

activities.why: Text in the middle briefing strip [[2:102|Chart Users' Guide p 102]]; hatched track, inset holding and profile icons [[2:115|Chart Users' Guide p 115]]; time/distance table below the sketch [[2:122|Chart Users' Guide p 122]]; higher gradients in the notes section [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]].

activities.title: Brief the Daggett missed approach
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin on the chart.

pins.label: Line that needs the 220 ft/NM climb

activities.why: The full text is in the middle briefing strip [[2:102|Chart Users' Guide p 102]], the track is hatched, holding fixes may be in an inset and the icons are in the profile [[2:115|Chart Users' Guide p 115]]. Details are from the chart [[29:187|IPH Figure 4-26]].

activities.title: True or false: is a missed approach required?
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: At the MAP with the REIL in sight, the published flight visibility and a normal descent available, the learner must go missed.
cards.why: False. REIL is a listed reference, so 91.175(c) is met [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(v)]].

cards.s: Circling at the MDA, losing sight of the airport only because of a normal bank requires a missed approach.
cards.why: False. 91.175(e)(2) excepts a loss of sight caused only by a normal bank [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]].

cards.s: With the runway in sight but flight visibility below the chart value, the learner must go missed even if the reported visibility is at minimums.
cards.why: True. Only the pilot judges flight visibility [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].

cards.s: On an LPV approach, the learner should wait for the along-track distance to reach zero before going missed.
cards.why: False. The missed starts at the DA and must not wait for the distance to reach zero [[33:106|AIM 1-1-18d7]].

cards.s: A RAIM alert after the FAWP calls for a climb and the missed approach.
When ATC instructs a missed approach, the pilot executes it.
cards.why: True. An ATC instruction is one of the listed conditions [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a1(c)]].

activities.title: Fly the missed approach
activities.intro: Put the first actions of a missed approach in order, then tap Check.
steps: Full power smoothly, carburetor heat off
Climb attitude, right rudder, rough trim
Descent stopped: flaps up in small steps
Positive rate of climb: gear up, if retractable
Turn as published, at or after the MAP
Advise ATC and request further clearance
activities.why: Power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]; gear after a positive rate of climb [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]; no turn before the MAP [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]; then advise ATC and request further clearance [[23:312|IFH 10-21]].

activities.title: Missed approach climb numbers
activities.intro: Work it out from the table or the chart, then type your answer.

items.q: The missed needs 297 ft/NM. Groundspeed on the climb will be 90 knots. What climb rate does the table give?
The missed needs 318 ft/NM at 120 knots groundspeed. What climb rate does the table give?
A chart needs 370 ft/NM. You planned 90 knots groundspeed, but a tailwind makes it 120 knots. How many more fpm does the table call for than you planned?
items.why: 3.5° row: 745 fpm at 120 knots minus 555 fpm at 90 knots = 190 fpm [[29:34|IPH Figure 1-17]]. A higher groundspeed raises the rate needed [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]].

items.q: Climbing at exactly 200 ft per NM, how many feet will the airplane gain in the first 3 NM?
items.why: The gradient is feet per NM: 3 × 200 = 600 ft [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. The IFH departure example uses the same idea: 200 ft/NM gives 400 ft at 2 NM [[23:61|IFH 2-10]].

items.q: Orlando LOC RWY 7: the FAF to MAP is 5.5 NM. At 120 knots groundspeed, how many seconds is it from the FAF to the MAP?
items.why: The chart table gives 2:45 at 120 knots, which is 165 seconds [[29:184|IPH Figure 4-23]]; start the clock at the FAF [[29:181|IPH 4-41]].

pairs.l: Going missed, weather now below minimums
Arriving at the missed approach holding fix
ILS receiver failed on the approach

pairs.l: Alternate missed needs DME you lack, issued after starting the approach
Unsure what a missed approach clearance means

activities.why: Phraseology from the IPH table [[29:105|IPH Figure 2-68]]; holding fix report [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(f)]]; malfunction report [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(a)]]; rejecting an alternate missed [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21e]]; uncertain of a clearance [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]].

activities.intro: Tap each situation, then tap the first thing the learner should do.
buckets: Fly to the MAP, then turn
Climbing turn toward the landing runway
Contact ATC for an amended clearance

items.t: Decides to go missed 2 NM before the MAP on a VOR approach
Activates the GPS missed before the MAWP
ATC says "go missed" 3 NM out with no other instructions
Loses the airport on downwind while circling
Loses the airport on base while circling in right traffic
Balked landing at 100 ft after passing the MAP
Rejected landing at 50 ft, past the MAP, for a deer on the runway

activities.why: Early missed: fly to the MAP before turning, unless ATC clears otherwise [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]], and do not turn before the MAWP [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(f)(1)]]. Lost while circling: climbing turn toward the landing runway [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]]. Balked or rejected landing away from the MAP, for example for animals on the runway [[29:180|IPH 4-40]]: contact ATC as soon as possible for an amended clearance [[33:452|AIM 5-4-21h]].

activities.title: Checkride: the examiner flies the missed approach errors
activities.intro: You are the CFII applicant. The examiner, playing your learner, flies the Orlando Executive LOC RWY 7 (Figure 4-23) under the device and makes errors on purpose. Choose what you say each time.

steps.s: Between the FAF and BUVAY at 1,600 ft, the examiner says "going missed" and climbs straight ahead toward 2,000.
options: Fine: any climb is safe once the missed starts
Name it: 1200 is the maximum; descend to it and fly to the MAP
Have the examiner turn left toward OVIDO now
Level at 1,600 until the MAP, then climb
steps.why: The missed is a climb to 1200 maximum and the note warns a descent to 1200 may be required on an early missed [[29:184|IPH Figure 4-23]]; comply with the maximum and fly to the MAP [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a4]].

steps.s: Back on profile, at the MAP the examiner adds full power and lets the nose rise steeply; the airspeed falls well below the climb speed.
options: Good: a steep pitch gains altitude fastest
Raise all the flaps to help the climb
Name it: improper pitch; forward pressure, climb attitude
Reduce power to stop the nose rising
steps.why: Hold forward pressure against the pitch-up from added power; a nose that rises too early can stall the airplane when low [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Improper pitch attitude is a listed go-around error [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

steps.s: Climbing, the examiner raises all the flaps at once and the VSI sags toward zero.
options: Name it: flaps up in small steps after the descent stops
Fine: drag must go as fast as possible
Lower the nose steeply to dive for speed
Lower the gear to steady the airplane
steps.why: A sudden, complete flap retraction can cause a loss of lift and settling; retract in small increments [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

steps.s: Passing 900 ft, the examiner has said nothing to the tower.
options: Fine: the tower can see the missed
Wait until reaching the holding fix
Only report the altitude being climbed to
Name it: no report; missed approach, reason, request
steps.why: Advise ATC of the missed and the reason, then request a specific action [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a2]] [[34:5|AIM 5-5-5a6]].

steps.s: At SOTCO the examiner turns right toward the ORL R-049 and OVIDO.
options: Fine: either turn reaches OVIDO
Name it: the published missed is a climbing left turn
Hold the heading and wait for vectors
Climb to 2,000 first, then turn either way
steps.why: The missed is a climbing left turn to 1500 via ORL R-049 to OVIDO [[29:184|IPH Figure 4-23]]; comply with the published missed unless ATC specifies another [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a3]].
